title: Quantizing gauge algebras that close modulo field equations
notes: The speaker mentions gauge transformations whose commutators close only after using equations of motion, and a Vilkovisky-related method.
statement: For fields \(\phi^i\) and gauge generators \(R^i_\alpha\), an open algebra has \([R_\alpha,R_\beta]^i=R^i_\gamma f^\gamma_{\alpha\beta}+M^{ij}_{\alpha\beta}\,\delta S/\delta\phi^j\). The Batalin–Vilkovisky method introduces ghosts and antifields and seeks an extended action satisfying the classical master equation \((S_{\mathrm{BV}},S_{\mathrm{BV}})=0\), with suitable properness and reducibility data. Open closure occurs in supergravity; ordinary spacetime diffeomorphisms already close off shell and should not be used as the universal example.
reconstruction: The master-equation formulation identifies the method; no unrecorded quantization theorem for the unspecified model is attributed to the seminar.
fate: Batalin and Vilkovisky (1983), abstract and pp. 2567–2582, explicitly address dependent generators and open algebras; the publisher abstract was opened. The earlier Fradkin–Vilkovisky (1975), pp. 224–226, constraint-quantization paper is another relevant bibliographic pointer, but its full text was not read.
present_status: Established under the explicitly stated assumptions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Clarifies the hypotheses and the distinction between a classical construction and a quantum assertion.

title: Superspaces, homogeneous maps, and block matrices
notes: The report starts with a vector space decomposed into two parity components and the corresponding parity of linear maps.
statement: Over a field of characteristic zero, a superspace is \(V=V_{\overline0}\oplus V_{\overline1}\). A homogeneous map \(T\) has parity \(|T|\in\mathbb Z/2\) when \(T(V_i)\subset V_{i+|T|}\). For \(V=\mathbb C^{m|n}\), even endomorphisms are block diagonal and odd endomorphisms block off-diagonal; all endomorphisms are sums of these components.
fate: Leites (1980), Chapter I, \S\S1.1–1.3, gives these definitions. They are background rather than a new classification result.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: Koszul signs and the Lie superalgebra identities
notes: The signs in skew symmetry and the Jacobi identity are discussed, with a reference to Quillen’s sign rule.
statement: For homogeneous \(x,y,z\), a Lie superbracket has parity \(|[x,y]|=|x|+|y|\), satisfies \([x,y]=-(-1)^{|x||y|}[y,x]\), and obeys \((-1)^{|x||z|}[x,[y,z]]+(-1)^{|y||x|}[y,[z,x]]+(-1)^{|z||y|}[z,[x,y]]=0\). Interchanging homogeneous tensor factors contributes \((-1)^{|x||y|}\).
fate: Leites (1980), Chapter I, \S1.9.1, states the identities, and the historical introduction discusses the sign convention. Earlier occurrences include 1976-404.1.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: The associative supercommutator
notes: An associative superalgebra is turned into a Lie superalgebra by a modified commutator.
statement: If \(A=A_{\overline0}\oplus A_{\overline1}\) is an associative algebra whose multiplication preserves parity, then \([x,y]=xy-(-1)^{|x||y|}yx\) for homogeneous elements extends bilinearly to a Lie superbracket. For \(A=\operatorname{End}(V)\) this gives \(\mathfrak{gl}(V)\). Associativity proves the super-Jacobi identity by cancellation of the six ordered triple products.
fate: This construction is explicit in Leites (1980), Chapter I, \S1.9.1, and is already implicit in earlier superalgebra records.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: Supertrace, special linear superalgebra, and Euler characteristic
notes: The difference of the two block traces is introduced and compared with an Euler characteristic.
statement: For \(X=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}\), define \(\operatorname{str}X=\operatorname{tr}A-\operatorname{tr}D\). It vanishes on supercommutators; hence \(\mathfrak{sl}(m|n)=\ker\operatorname{str}\) is a Lie subsuperalgebra. For a finite complex with even chain endomorphism \(T\), the alternating trace on chain spaces equals the alternating trace induced on cohomology; for \(T=1\) this is the Euler characteristic.
reconstruction: Finiteness and the chain-map hypothesis are added to make the Euler-characteristic analogy an actual trace identity.
fate: Leites (1980), Chapter I, \S1.6, supplies supertrace; the cohomological equality follows by splitting cycles and boundaries in a finite complex. The simplicity of \(\mathfrak{sl}(m|n)\) is not automatic when \(m=n\), where scalar matrices lie in its center.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: Classical and vector-field families
notes: The list includes linear, orthogonal, symplectic, and vector-field families denoted \(W,S,H,K\).
statement: The list names several different constructions. For example \(W(n)=\operatorname{Der}\Lambda(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)\) is finite dimensional when all \(n\) coordinates are odd; allowing even polynomial or formal coordinates produces infinite-dimensional vector-field superalgebras. Divergence, symplectic, or contact preservation yields the corresponding special, Hamiltonian, or contact families, with simplicity requiring the appropriate derived algebra and rank hypotheses.
reconstruction: The example (W(n)) fixes one category; no uniform unqualified simplicity claim is attached to the entire list.
fate: Kac (1977), A sketch of Lie superalgebra theory, pp. 31–64, classifies simple finite-dimensional examples; its publisher abstract was opened, but the full classification proof was not read. The notebook list is not an exhaustive theorem across all finite, polynomial, and formal categories.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: Orthosymplectic algebras from an even form
notes: Preservation of a nondegenerate graded form is used to define an orthosymplectic family.
statement: Let \(V=\mathbb C^{m|2n}\) carry a nondegenerate even supersymmetric bilinear form \(B\): it is symmetric on \(V_{\overline0}\), alternating on \(V_{\overline1}\), and vanishes on mixed parity. The homogeneous endomorphisms satisfying \(B(Xv,w)+(-1)^{|X||v|}B(v,Xw)=0\) form \(\mathfrak{osp}(m|2n)\), whose even part is \(\mathfrak{so}(m)\oplus\mathfrak{sp}(2n)\).
fate: Leites (1980), Chapter I, \S1.5, gives the graded bilinear-form conventions. The intrinsic identity avoids ambiguity among supertranspose conventions in block notation.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: The periplectic algebra
notes: The family denoted \(\Pi(n)\) is displayed in blocks with one symmetric and one skew-symmetric off-diagonal block.
statement: With one standard convention, the periplectic algebra preserving a nondegenerate odd symmetric form on \(\mathbb C^{n|n}\) is \(\mathfrak{pe}(n)=\{\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&-A^{t}\end{pmatrix}:B^{t}=B,\ C^{t}=-C\}\). Its special subalgebra imposes \(\operatorname{tr}A=0\); this special algebra is simple for \(n\ge3\). A parity reversal of the form interchanges the symmetric and alternating block conventions.
reconstruction: The notation \(\Pi(n)\) is normalized to \(\mathfrak{pe}(n)\); the special-algebra and rank qualifications are supplied explicitly.
fate: This is one of the classical matrix families in Kac’s 1977 classification. The classification citation was verified at publisher-metadata level; the displayed block condition itself is checked by preserving the odd form.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: The queer algebra as a supercentralizer
notes: An odd complex structure \(J\) and matrices with equal diagonal and off-diagonal blocks are written.
statement: Let \(J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}\) on \(\mathbb C^{n|n}\). Its supercentralizer consists of \(\mathfrak q(n)=\{\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B&A\end{pmatrix}\}\): an even matrix commutes with \(J\), while an odd one anticommutes with it. The bracket is the supercommutator, not an ordinary commutator on arbitrary inhomogeneous matrices.
fate: The queer family is classical background included in Kac (1977); Leites’s general matrix and parity conventions explain the centralizer condition. The block calculation is immediate from the displayed \(J\).
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: Queer trace and the central quotient
notes: A trace of the off-diagonal block is defined, with a purported equality to a supertrace involving \(J\).
statement: For \(X=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B&A\end{pmatrix}\), the odd linear functional \(\operatorname{qtr}X=\operatorname{tr}B\) vanishes on supercommutators. Thus \(\mathfrak{sq}(n)=\ker\operatorname{qtr}\) is a subsuperalgebra. For \(n\ge3\), \(\mathfrak{psq}(n)=\mathfrak{sq}(n)/\mathbb CI\) is simple. With the preceding \(J\), however, \(\operatorname{str}(XJ)=-2\operatorname{tr}B\), so \(\operatorname{qtr}X=-\frac12\operatorname{str}(XJ)\).
fate: The family and its special central quotient are standard classification data. The normalization correction follows by multiplying the two displayed block matrices and does not depend on later literature. A final scan check of the handwritten normalization was prevented by the outage, so the correction is against the supplied transcription.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: Gelfand’s question about Jordan form
notes: Gelfand asks whether there is a Jordan-form theorem in this setting.
statement: A classification problem would need to specify whether the operator is even or odd, whether its entries lie in \(\mathbb C\) or a supercommutative base algebra, and which parity-preserving or supergroup conjugations are allowed. These alternatives produce different problems; none is fixed in the surviving question.
fate: Searches for Leites, Gelfand, Jordan form, and supermatrices did not identify an exact published answer to this particular formulation. Work on Jordan superalgebras is a different subject and was not accepted as a match.
present_status: The question remains insufficiently specified for an exact problem/status assignment.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: The exceptional algebra F(4)
notes: An exceptional algebra is described using an orthogonal algebra, an \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) factor, and a spin representation.
statement: The complex exceptional simple Lie superalgebra \(F(4)\) has even part \(\mathfrak{so}_7\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_2\) and odd part \(\operatorname{Spin}_7\otimes\mathbb C^2\), where \(\operatorname{Spin}_7\) denotes the eight-dimensional spin module. Its superdimension is \(24|16\). The equivariant odd-odd bracket is normalized so that the super-Jacobi identity holds.
fate: This is the exceptional family in Kac’s 1977 classification; the old notation in the notes is identified by its even part and odd module, not by typography alone. The classification article was checked through its publisher metadata, not read in full.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: The one-parameter exceptional family D(2,1;alpha)
notes: Three two-dimensional symplectic spaces and coefficients whose sum is zero are used to construct an exceptional family.
statement: Let \((V_i,\psi_i)\), \(i=1,2,3\), be two-dimensional complex symplectic spaces. Put \(\mathfrak g_{\overline0}=\bigoplus_i\mathfrak{sp}(V_i)\), \(\mathfrak g_{\overline1}=V_1\otimes V_2\otimes V_3\). Define \(P_i(x,y)z=\psi_i(y,z)x+\psi_i(x,z)y\). The odd bracket is \(\sum_i\sigma_i\psi_j(x_j,y_j)\psi_k(x_k,y_k)P_i(x_i,y_i)\), where \(\{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}\). It satisfies Jacobi exactly when \(\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3=0\); it is simple when every \(\sigma_i\ne0\). Common rescaling and permutation of the triple yield the isomorphisms; a normalized ratio gives \(D(2,1;\alpha)\), \(\alpha\notin\{0,-1\}\).
reconstruction: The bracket is written once for each of the three factors, avoiding an unnormalized sum over all six permutations.
fate: Poletaeva (2010), \S2, equations (1)–(5), explicitly records this construction, Jacobi condition, simplicity criterion, and parameter equivalence, attributing the equivalent presentation to Scheunert. This verifies the exact mathematical content; it is not evidence that the family first appeared in 2010. Kac’s classification predates the seminar.
present_status: Classical superalgebraic background, already known before the 1984 report and still valid with the stated conventions on 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes parity, characteristic, and matrix conventions explicit.

title: Flag stabilizers and parity sequences
notes: For \(SL(n|m)\), the report describes different Borels by strings of \(n\) plus signs and \(m\) minus signs.
statement: Let \(G=SL(n|m)\) over \(\mathbb C\), \(n,m>0\), \(n\ne m\). A complete flag in the free superspace has successive quotients of rank \(1|0\) or \(0|1\). Its parity sequence \(J\) has \(n\) even and \(m\) odd entries. The stabilizer \(B_J\) is a triangular Borel subsupergroup; up to conjugacy by the even group, these choices are classified by their parity sequences. This definition must not be replaced without qualification by “maximal solvable subsuperalgebra.”
fate: Penkov (1988), \S1.2, develops the Borel and flag conventions. Manin and Voronov (1988/1990), introduction and \S1, explicitly warn that the ordinary maximal-solvable characterization does not transfer unchanged to supergroups.
present_status: Established with the stated hypotheses as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: Dimension and reduced space of a complete superflag
notes: The flag space \(G/B_J\) is used as the geometric carrier of the representation.
statement: The reduced variety of the complete flag superspace is \(\operatorname{Fl}(\mathbb C^n)\times\operatorname{Fl}(\mathbb C^m)\). Its superdimension is \(\bigl(n(n-1)/2+m(m-1)/2\,\big|\,nm\bigr)\), independently of the ordering \(J\), although the full superspace and its sheaf of functions depend on \(J\).
fate: The flag construction is given in Manin and Voronov, \S1; the dimension follows by counting positive even and odd roots. Equality of reduced spaces does not imply isomorphism of the superspaces.
present_status: Established with the stated hypotheses as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: Characters and equivariant line bundles
notes: Line bundles are identified with characters of a Cartan or Borel subgroup.
statement: For a fixed \(B_J\) and its diagonal torus \(T\), even \(G\)-equivariant line bundles on \(G/B_J\) are classified by algebraic characters of \(B_J\), equivalently characters of \(T\), through the associated-bundle construction. One must specify equivariance and parity. This statement alone does not identify the entire ordinary Picard group of an arbitrary supermanifold.
reconstruction: Only the justified equivariant Picard assertion is used; no unverified claim about all non-equivariant super line bundles is added.
fate: Penkov (1988), \S1, constructs the homogeneous sheaves from inducing representations. The precise character statement is standard homogeneous-bundle theory; the notebook’s bare Picard notation requires the equivariance qualification.
present_status: Established with the stated hypotheses as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: The typical Borel–Weil–Bott theorem
notes: The displayed theorem excludes odd-root hyperplanes and places cohomology in one Weyl-group degree.
statement: Let \(B\) be a triangular Borel of \(SL(n|m)\), \(n\ne m\), and \(\mathcal L_\lambda=G\times_B\mathbb C_{-\lambda}\) an even homogeneous line bundle for an integral character. Put \(\rho_B=\frac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta^+_{\overline0}}\alpha-\frac12\sum_{\beta\in\Delta^+_{\overline1}}\beta\) and \(\chi=\lambda+\rho_B\). Assume \((\chi,\beta)\ne0\) for every odd root \(\beta\). If \(\chi\) is even-singular, all cohomology vanishes. If \(\chi\) is even-regular, let \(w\in S_n\times S_m\) send it into the dominant even chamber. Exactly degree \(\ell(w)\) can be nonzero, and that cohomology is irreducible. For the distinguished Borel, its contragredient has highest weight \(w\chi-\rho_B\); for other parity sequences one transports the highest weight and parity by odd reflections.
reconstruction: The bundle sign and contragredient convention are stated explicitly. Atypical weights are outside the theorem; no vanishing statement is inferred for them. The simplified highest-weight formula is restricted to the distinguished Borel.
fate: Penkov (1988), \S2.1, Theorem 1, Russian p. 93, states and proves the typical theorem. The early Penkov–Skornyakov announcement is C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 299 (1984), 1005–1008; that original note was identified but not read. The 1988 Russian treatment appeared in English in 1990.
present_status: Established with the stated hypotheses as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: Changing a Borel by an odd reflection
notes: The weight notation is shifted by a parity-sequence-dependent \(\rho_J\), and the different flags are compared.
statement: If an isotropic odd simple root \(\beta\) is reflected, then the positive-root system changes by \(\beta\mapsto-\beta\) and \(\rho_{B'}=\rho_B+\beta\). For a typical irreducible module, the highest weight changes from \(\lambda\) to \(\lambda-\beta\), and a highest vector changes parity. Thus \(\lambda+\rho_B\) is preserved; unqualified equality of graded representations across all flags omits a parity choice.
fate: Penkov (1988), \S1.2 and the odd-reflection steps in the proof of \S2.1, gives the mechanism underlying the flag-dependent notation. This is a method in the proved typical theory, not a claim that all superflags are isomorphic.
present_status: Established with the stated hypotheses as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: The repeated typical cohomology statement
notes: The line-bundle theorem from 19 March is restated with the shifted weight \(\chi-\rho_J\).
statement: With the hypotheses and conventions of item 1983-627.4, the cohomology of the corresponding homogeneous line bundle is zero for even-singular \(\chi\), and otherwise is concentrated in degree \(\ell(w)\), with an irreducible typical module. Character integrality, the odd-root nonvanishing condition, and the even Weyl-group regularity are separate requirements.
reconstruction: The earlier item supplies the precise convention; the repeated notebook formula is not used to erase parity or contragredient issues.
fate: This is a second occurrence of the same typical theorem, matched to Penkov (1988), \S2.1, Theorem 1. It is not a new open question and receives no new problem identifier.
present_status: Established with the stated hypotheses as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: The announced differential-operator version
notes: The speaker says there is also a version involving \(D\)-modules.
statement: The identifiable direction is to relate representations to sheaves of differential operators on superflag varieties. A precise equivalence would require a twisting parameter, a specified module category, and regularity or typicality assumptions. The record does not state these data or an equivalence theorem.
reconstruction: The defined direction is matched bibliographically; the notebook does not state enough hypotheses to reproduce the full later theorem.
fate: Penkov (1988), bibliography item 22, explicitly identifies Penkov–Skornyakov, Cohomologie des D-modules tordus typiques sur les supervarietes de drapeaux, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 299 (1984), 1005–1008. Its title matches this announcement; the original note was not obtained. Bibliography item 21 separately identifies Penkov’s 1987 localization note. Thus the direction has a concrete published continuation, while its exact category-equivalence hypotheses remain unverified here.
present_status: An exact contemporary paper on typical twisted D-module cohomology is identified, but its full theorem was not read; no unverified localization equivalence is asserted.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: Flags with volume data and the space G/N
notes: Flags are supplemented with forms of volume, and an affine flag space is described.
statement: For an ordinary connected reductive group \(G\), a Borel \(B=TN\), and unipotent radical \(N\), the quotient \(G/N\to G/B\) is a principal \(T\)-bundle; for \(SL_r\), it can be interpreted as complete flags with compatible nonzero determinant data on their subspaces. Its analogous super construction must use the appropriate Berezinian lines and parity conventions. This homogeneous space is distinct from an affine flag variety attached to a loop group.
reconstruction: The ordinary quotient is stated completely. The notebook’s super volume terminology is normalized to Berezinian data without claiming an unrecorded global theorem.
fate: The quotient construction is standard and supplies the precise ordinary case. Penkov’s and Manin–Voronov’s flag formalism provides the supergeometric setting; an exact unrestricted identification using ordinary volume forms in every odd direction is not asserted.
present_status: Established with the stated hypotheses as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: Monotone ranks in a flag and the underlying ordinary flags
notes: An example chain contains a step whose even rank decreases, and the even and odd flag components are illustrated.
statement: In a flag of locally free direct summands, both ranks are nondecreasing: \(V^{a|b}\subset V^{c|d}\) requires \(a\le c\) and \(b\le d\). Thus a chain \(T^{1|0}\subset T^{2|0}\subset T^{1|1}\) cannot be the intended flag; \(T^{2|1}\) is the natural next rank if the last step adds one odd dimension. The reduced full flag remains the product of the even and odd ordinary full flags.
reconstruction: The correction (2|1) is the minimal rank-compatible reconstruction; the original image should decide whether the error is scribal or transcriptional.
fate: This is a rank check, not a new theorem. The example is interpreted using the general flag definition in Manin and Voronov, \S1. The proposed corrected superscript is conditional on the supplied transcription because the final scan recheck was blocked.
present_status: Established with the stated hypotheses as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Separates the precise typical-weight theorem from statements that fail or require modification in supergeometry.

title: The six-generator derived affine algebra
notes: Six Chevalley generators and the affine \(2\times2\) Cartan matrix are written.
statement: Let \(A=(a_{ij})=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}\). Over \(\mathbb C\), impose \([h_i,h_j]=0\), \([h_i,e_j]=a_{ij}e_j\), \([h_i,f_j]=-a_{ij}f_j\), \([e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}h_i\), and \((\operatorname{ad}e_i)^3e_j=(\operatorname{ad}f_i)^3f_j=0\) for \(i\ne j\). This gives \(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2'=(\mathfrak{sl}_2\otimes\mathbb C[t,t^{-1}])\oplus\mathbb Cc\), with \(c=h_1+h_2\). The loop-degree derivation is an additional generator, absent from this presentation.
fate: Malikov, Feigin, and Fuchs (1986), \S1 and opening of \S3, use this exact presentation. The distinction between the derived algebra and its extension by a derivation is necessary.
present_status: Established with the stated algebraic conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Resolves the highest-versus-lowest-weight convention and distinguishes finite algebraic expressions from formal completions.

title: Highest- and lowest-weight Verma modules
notes: The generating vector in the notebook is killed by the negative generators.
statement: For a highest-weight convention, \(M(\mu)=U(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2')\otimes_{U(\mathfrak h+\mathfrak n_+)}\mathbb C_\mu\), where \(e_i v_\mu=0\) and \(h_i v_\mu=\mu_i v_\mu\). As a vector space it is \(U(\mathfrak n_-)v_\mu\). The notebook’s convention \(f_i v=0\), \(h_i v=\lambda_i v\) is lowest weight; the Chevalley involution \(e_i\leftrightarrow f_i,\ h_i\mapsto-h_i\) converts it to the highest weight \(\mu=-\lambda\).
reconstruction: The two definitions are both legitimate; only mixing their parameter signs is erroneous.
fate: Malikov–Feigin–Fuchs (1986), \S1, defines the highest-weight convention used in its formulas. The conversion is algebraic and must precede comparison with the notebook.
present_status: Established with the stated algebraic conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Resolves the highest-versus-lowest-weight convention and distinguishes finite algebraic expressions from formal completions.

title: Reducibility and nontrivial singular vectors
notes: Reducibility is related to a vector annihilated by the same nilpotent subalgebra as the vacuum.
statement: A root-graded Verma module is reducible if and only if it contains a nonzero singular vector not proportional to its generating vector. In highest-weight notation this means \(e_1w=e_2w=0\), \(w\notin\mathbb Cv_\mu\); in the lowest-weight convention the \(f_i\) replace the \(e_i\). The nontriviality condition is essential because the vacuum is always singular.
fate: Malikov–Feigin–Fuchs (1986), \S1, immediately before Theorem 1.1, states this criterion. The root grading, or an extension by the degree derivation, keeps the positive-height argument distinct from the degenerate affine Cartan weight alone.
present_status: Established with the stated algebraic conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Resolves the highest-versus-lowest-weight convention and distinguishes finite algebraic expressions from formal completions.

title: The affine sl2 reducibility hyperplanes
notes: The notebook gives two families of affine-linear equations and a critical-level equation, but permits \(n=0\).
statement: In the highest-weight convention, \(M(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) is reducible precisely if, for some integer \(k\ge0\), either \((k+1)(\mu_1+1)+k(\mu_2+1)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), or \(k(\mu_1+1)+(k+1)(\mu_2+1)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), or \(\mu_1+\mu_2+2=0\). In the notebook’s lowest-weight convention substitute \(\mu_i=-\lambda_i\); the critical equation becomes \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2=2\). Zero is excluded from the real-root integer condition.
reconstruction: The notebook’s signs and its \(n\ge0\) condition cannot both be retained with its lowest-weight definition.
fate: Malikov–Feigin–Fuchs (1986), \S3, Proposition 3.1, Russian p. 29, states the exact specialization of the earlier Kac–Kazhdan criterion. Its indexing uses \(k>0\); replacing \(k\) by \(k+1\) gives the displayed form. The paper’s \S1, Theorem 1.1, identifies the earlier result.
present_status: Established with the stated algebraic conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Resolves the highest-versus-lowest-weight convention and distinguishes finite algebraic expressions from formal completions.

title: Casimir polynomials and the completion issue
notes: Gelfand asks about Casimir expressions in the generators.
statement: On the literal finite-polynomial reading, the question is the center of \(U(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2')\), and the answer is \(\mathbb C[c]\). If infinite normally ordered expressions or their action at fixed level are intended, a topology and level must instead be specified. These are different algebraic questions.
reconstruction: The PBW argument is our annotation, not an attribution of a new theorem or of the later completed-center theory to the seminar. No new open-problem ID is assigned to the ambiguous remainder.
fate: The finite-polynomial answer has an elementary PBW proof: the highest symbol of a central element is a polynomial in finitely many loop modes. Commuting with a mode of sufficiently large degree gives independent new mode variables; their coefficients force every derivative with respect to the original \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) modes to vanish, since \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) has zero center. The symbol depends only on \(c\), and induction on PBW degree gives \(\mathbb C[c]\). Frenkel (2007), \S2.1.2 and \S3.5, concerns the different completed question; \S4.3, Proposition 4.3.9, gives the scalar center away from critical level.
present_status: The finite-polynomial interpretation is answered by the elementary argument; the precise intended completed or representation-level Casimir question is not determined by the short record.
worth: Resolves the highest-versus-lowest-weight convention and distinguishes finite algebraic expressions from formal completions.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: The Malikov–Feigin–Fuchs singular-vector product
notes: Products with nonintegral exponents are proposed as a way to write singular vectors.
statement: For integers \(n,k>0\) and \(t\in\mathbb C\), let \(F(n,k,t)\) be the alternating product of \(2k-1\) factors beginning and ending with \(f_1\), with exponents \(n+(k-1)t,n+(k-2)t,\ldots,n-(k-1)t\). For \(\mu_1=n-1-(k-1)t\), \(\mu_2=-n-1+kt\), this formal product has a well-defined value in \(U(\mathfrak n_-)\), and \(F(n,k,t)v_\mu\) is a singular vector of degree \(n(k\alpha_1+(k-1)\alpha_2)\). Interchanging the two simple roots gives the other family.
reconstruction: The precise product length, parameter restrictions, and highest-weight convention are supplied from the matched theorem.
fate: Malikov, Feigin, and Fuchs (1986), \S3, Theorem 3.2, equations (6)–(7), is an exact match; the paper was received 26 December 1984. It proves that the formal expression becomes an ordinary enveloping-algebra element rather than treating arbitrary complex powers as analytic operators.
present_status: Established with the stated algebraic conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Resolves the highest-versus-lowest-weight convention and distinguishes finite algebraic expressions from formal completions.

title: Generalized binomial commutation
notes: A generalized commutator formula is used to manipulate nonintegral powers.
statement: If the iterated right commutators \(D_y^j(x)=[\cdots[[x,y],y],\ldots,y]\) eventually vanish, the formal rule \([x,y^z]=\sum_{j\ge1}\binom zj y^{z-j}D_y^j(x)\) is finite. For integer \(z\ge0\) it follows by induction; polynomial continuation of the coefficients defines the formal-power calculation in a suitable localization or ordered-symbol algebra. It does not define a complex power of every operator in every representation.
fate: Malikov–Feigin–Fuchs (1986), \S2, Propositions 2.1–2.2, and the universal formula (8) in the proof of Theorem 3.2 provide the exact computational method.
present_status: Established with the stated algebraic conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Resolves the highest-versus-lowest-weight convention and distinguishes finite algebraic expressions from formal completions.

title: Pure real Hodge structures
notes: The report defines a decomposition indexed by two integers and a conjugation condition.
statement: A pure real Hodge structure of weight \(n\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space \(H_{\mathbb R}\) with \(H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}\) and \(\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}\). Equivalently, a finite decreasing filtration \(F\) satisfies \(H_{\mathbb C}=F^pH_{\mathbb C}\oplus\overline{F^{n-p+1}H_{\mathbb C}}\) for every \(p\).
fate: Deligne (1971), \S2.1, supplies the classical definition. Bunke, Nikolaus, and Tamme (2018), Definition 2.1, states the real version with these conventions.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: Mixed real Hodge structures
notes: The direct-sum picture is modified by a weight filtration and a conjugation condition modulo lower terms.
statement: A mixed real Hodge structure is a finite-dimensional \(H_{\mathbb R}\), a finite increasing real filtration \(W\), and a finite decreasing filtration \(F\) on \(H_{\mathbb C}\), such that the induced \(F\) on \(\operatorname{gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\) defines a pure real Hodge structure of weight \(n\) for every \(n\). Exhaustiveness and separatedness are included in “finite filtration.”
fate: Deligne (1971), \S2.3, defines mixed Hodge structures. Bunke–Nikolaus–Tamme (2018), Definition 2.2, gives the same real-coefficient convention.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: Deligne’s canonical complex bigrading
notes: A bigrading is used to represent the mixed structure and to compare it with its conjugate.
statement: There is a unique functorial decomposition \(H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus I^{p,q}\) with \(F^p=\bigoplus_{r\ge p}I^{r,s}\), \(W_n=\bigoplus_{r+s\le n}I^{r,s}\), and \(\overline{I^{p,q}}\equiv I^{q,p}\pmod{\bigoplus_{r<q,\ s<p}I^{r,s}}\). This splits \(W\) over \(\mathbb C\) compatibly with \(F\). The summands need not be conjugate exactly, so this decomposition does not identify the original mixed Hodge structure with a direct sum of pure real structures.
reconstruction: The strict inequalities in the conjugation remainder specify the otherwise compressed phrase “lower terms.”
fate: Deligne (1971), \S1.2, Lemma 1.2.11, constructs the two functorial complex bigradings used in the mixed-Hodge setting of \S2.3. The conjugation refinement is the standard Deligne splitting convention; it must not be confused with a real splitting preserving the original Hodge filtration.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: Real splitting and exactness in the category
notes: Split structures are contrasted with general mixed structures, and categorical properties are discussed.
statement: A mixed real Hodge structure is split over \(\mathbb R\) precisely when its canonical bigrading satisfies \(\overline{I^{p,q}}=I^{q,p}\); then it is a direct sum of pure real Hodge structures. Morphisms preserving \(W\) and \(F\) are strict for both filtrations, and kernels and cokernels with induced filtrations make the category \(\mathrm{MHS}_{\mathbb R}\) abelian. A functorial real splitting obtained by changing \(F\) must not be confused with an isomorphism preserving the original \(F\).
fate: Deligne (1971), \S2.3, Corollary 2.3.5, gives strictness and the abelian-category statement; the splitting condition follows from the bigrading.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: Mixed Hodge structures on algebraic cohomology
notes: Cohomology of algebraic varieties is given as the main source of mixed Hodge structures.
statement: For a separated complex algebraic variety of finite type, each singular cohomology group \(H^j(X,\mathbb R)\) has a functorial mixed real Hodge structure. If \(X\) is smooth and projective, this structure is pure of weight \(j\). Singularities and nonproperness generally require mixed weights.
fate: Deligne (1971), Theorem 3.2.5(iii) and Definition 3.2.12, treats the smooth nonproper case; Deligne (1974), Proposition 8.2.2, proves the general separated finite-type construction and functoriality. These results predate the seminar.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: The operator comparing conjugate splittings
notes: An operator called arithmetic monodromy compares a splitting with its conjugate and is said to become trivial in the split case.
statement: Put \(J^{p,q}=\overline{I^{q,p}}\). Both \(I\) and \(J\) split the same weight-graded Hodge spaces. Define \(T\) to carry \(I^{p,q}\) to \(J^{p,q}\) by the identity on \(\operatorname{gr}^W_{p+q}\). Then \(T\) is unipotent, \((T-1)I^{p,q}\subset\bigoplus_{r<p,\ s<q}I^{r,s}\), and \(\overline T=T^{-1}\). In particular \((T-1)W_n\subset W_{n-2}\), and \(T=1\) exactly for a structure split over \(\mathbb R\).
reconstruction: The operator is defined explicitly from the two splittings. This supplies a precise interpretation of the notebook terminology without asserting that Deligne uses that name.
fate: These assertions follow directly from the canonical bigrading and its conjugation condition in Deligne’s splitting formalism. The term “arithmetic monodromy” in the notebook is not identified with topological monodromy of a family or with the nilpotent operator of a degeneration.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: Rational and integral coefficient structures
notes: The coefficient ring is allowed to be \(\mathbb Z\), \(\mathbb Q\), or \(\mathbb R\).
statement: For rational coefficients, replace \(H_{\mathbb R}\) by a finite-dimensional rational vector space with rational \(W\), and impose the Hodge condition after tensoring with \(\mathbb R\) and \(\mathbb C\). An integral structure additionally specifies a finitely generated lattice; if only free lattices are allowed, the resulting category is not abelian under arbitrary cokernels. Statements about integral Ext therefore require an explicit convention about torsion and the exact category.
reconstruction: The torsion qualification is added because the notebook varies the coefficient ring without separately defining each homological category.
fate: Deligne’s coefficient conventions explain the rational and integral forms. The real Ext computation later in this report is not silently asserted unchanged in every integral category.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: Tate objects and the sign of the Hodge type
notes: The rank-one object \(A(i)=(2\pi i)^iA\) is written with a Hodge bidegree.
statement: With the standard cohomological Tate convention, \(A(i)\) has Hodge type \((-i,-i)\) and weight \(-2i\), and tensoring by it changes bidegrees by \((p,q)\mapsto(p-i,q-i)\). A convention using type \((i,i)\) is the opposite twist \(A(-i)\); the period factor alone does not determine a sign convention unless the filtration is stated.
fate: Bunke–Nikolaus–Tamme (2018), Example 2.3, explicitly fixes the standard real Tate object and weight. The notebook’s opposite-looking bidegree is recorded as a convention ambiguity rather than automatically attributed to OCR.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: Absolute Hodge cohomology of a mixed structure
notes: Cohomology is defined using derived Hom from the trivial Hodge structure.
statement: For \(M\in\mathrm{MHS}_{\mathbb R}\), set \(H^i_{\mathrm H}(M)=\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\mathrm{MHS}_{\mathbb R}}(\mathbb R(0),M)\). The zeroth group is \(W_0M_{\mathbb R}\cap F^0M_{\mathbb C}\), viewed inside \(M_{\mathbb C}\). For a bounded complex \(K\) of mixed Hodge structures, use \(\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b(\mathrm{MHS}_{\mathbb R})}(\mathbb R(0),K[i])\).
fate: Beilinson’s absolute-Hodge construction was published in 1986. Bunke–Nikolaus–Tamme (2018), introduction and \S2, explicitly identifies this derived formulation and cites Beilinson’s Theorem 3.4. The original 1986 chapter was verified bibliographically but not read.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: The first Ext quotient and vanishing in higher degrees
notes: The quotient formula for \(H^1\) is set as an exercise, with vanishing above degree one.
statement: For every finite-dimensional real mixed Hodge structure \(M\), \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb R(0),M)\cong W_0M_{\mathbb C}/(W_0M_{\mathbb R}+(F^0M_{\mathbb C}\cap W_0M_{\mathbb C}))\), as a real vector space, and \(\operatorname{Ext}^i(\mathbb R(0),M)=0\) for \(i>1\). These groups are computed by the two-term complex \(W_0M_{\mathbb R}\oplus(F^0M_{\mathbb C}\cap W_0M_{\mathbb C})\to W_0M_{\mathbb C}\), \((a,b)\mapsto a-b\), in degrees \(0,1\).
reconstruction: The quotient is real-linear, not a quotient by complex vector subspaces. The exact checked assertion uses real coefficients.
fate: Bunke–Nikolaus–Tamme (2018), Construction 2.8, equation (8), and Proposition 2.10, give the mapping-complex model; specialize its first argument to \(\mathbb R(0)\) and the second to a degree-zero structure. This directly verifies both the quotient and the higher vanishing. The original Beilinson chapter’s corresponding proof was not read.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: A derived Hodge object for an algebraic variety
notes: The report aims to attach complexes with Hodge coefficients to varieties, in analogy with other cohomological formalisms.
statement: For a smooth complex algebraic variety \(X\), the absolute-Hodge formalism supplies an object \(R\Gamma_{\mathrm H}(X)\) in the derived category of mixed real Hodge structures whose cohomology is the ordinary cohomology of \(X\) with its mixed Hodge structure. One defines \(H^n_{\mathrm{abs}}(X,\mathbb R(p))=\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b(\mathrm{MHS}_{\mathbb R})}(\mathbb R(0),R\Gamma_{\mathrm H}(X)(p)[n])\). A chosen chain-level model is additional data.
reconstruction: The smooth-variety case is stated precisely; the notebook’s wider analogy is not expanded into unrecorded comparison theorems.
fate: Beilinson (1986), Théorem 3.4, is identified by Bunke–Nikolaus–Tamme (2018), Proposition 2.7, as the derived equivalence between complexes of mixed Hodge structures and mixed Hodge complexes. Their \S3 constructs a concrete absolute-Hodge model for smooth varieties. The original chapter was not read, so its exact result is verified indirectly through this explicit primary reuse.
present_status: Established with real coefficients and the stated filtration conventions as of 12 November 2026.
worth: Makes coefficient, weight, and derived-category conventions explicit without turning an exercise into an open problem.

title: Finite-volume Ising Gibbs measure
notes: The notes introduce spins \(\sigma_x=\pm1\) and a Gibbs weight determined by pair interactions and inverse temperature.
statement: On finite \(\Lambda\), with specified boundary condition, \(P_\beta(\sigma)=Z_{\Lambda,\beta}^{-1}\exp(\beta\sum_{\{x,y\}}J_{xy}\sigma_x\sigma_y)\); a field term may be added but is set to zero in the subsequent critical discussion.
fate: Classical model definition, long before the talk. Infinite-volume statements require an indicated Gibbs state.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026: Classical model definition, long before the talk. Infinite-volume statements require an indicated Gibbs state.

title: Subcritical exponential decay
notes: At high temperature the spin correlation is said to decay exponentially.
statement: For nonnegative translation-invariant finite-range couplings on \(\mathbb Z^d\), the zero-field two-point function satisfies \(\langle\sigma_0\sigma_x\rangle_\beta\le e^{-c(\beta)|x|}\) for \(\beta<\beta_c\), with a harmless metric-dependent constant convention.
fate: The general-dimensional sharpness theorem was proved after the talk (Aizenman--Barsky--Fernandez, 1987, as identified by Duminil-Copin--Tassion). The latter paper's Ising Theorem 2.1(3), not its percolation Theorem 1.1, is the verified modern statement. Planar exact-model antecedents do not establish the general version.

title: Ordered phase and spontaneous magnetization
notes: The low-temperature correlation has a nonzero long-distance limit; the critical inequality is compressed.
statement: For the square-lattice ferromagnetic nearest-neighbour model in the ordered phase \(\beta>\beta_c\), the long-distance two-point limit is \(m(\beta)^2>0\). At the critical point the spontaneous magnetization vanishes.
fate: Yang's 1952 magnetization formula is earlier than the seminar. The ordered-phase statement requires the strict inequality and a specified infinite-volume state.

title: Critical exponent and singular free energy
notes: A power law with exponent \(1/4\) and the distinction from the ordered/disordered regimes are stated.
statement: At criticality in the planar nearest-neighbour model the two-point correlation decays as an amplitude times \(|x-y|^{-1/4}\); the exact free energy has its classical critical singularity.
fate: The exact square-lattice results predate the talk (Onsager; Wu--McCoy--Tracy--Barouch). This does not justify the same exponent for an arbitrary interaction.

title: Joint block-magnetization limit
notes: The seminar asks for simultaneous limits of rescaled sums over several regions.
statement: For bounded regular blocks \(B_j\) in the critical planar nearest-neighbour model, seek a joint limit of \(L^{-15/8}\sum_{x/L\in B_j}\sigma_x\), with consistent lattice amplitude and boundary conditions.
fate: Camia--Garban--Newman constructed the magnetization field and compatible block limits: 2012 preprint, 2015 journal, Theorem 1.3, Corollary 1.6 and Appendix A. Generalized-field convergence and block observables are distinguished.

title: Universality of the critical limiting field
notes: The joint limit is expected not to depend on the initial model; its class and normalization are unstated.
statement: For zero-field, translation-invariant, square-symmetric, finite-range ferromagnetic pair interactions on \(\mathbb Z^2\) with connected interaction graph, establish the critical bulk magnetization-field limit and its identification with the nearest-neighbour field after a model-dependent multiplicative normalization. The notebook does not specify this class; it is an explicit editorial reconstruction.

title: Renormalization as a pushforward transformation
notes: Block variables and repeated changes of scale are used to compare models.

fate: The method and epsilon-expansion programme were already established by Wilson and collaborators. The 1974 review is a bibliographic match, but direct full-text access failed in this run.

title: Unique centre of a bounded Hilbert set
notes: The notes use the centre of a bounded set in a Hilbert space.
statement: Every nonempty bounded subset \(A\) of a real or complex Hilbert space is contained in a unique closed ball of minimum radius; no compactness of \(A\) is needed.

notes: The centre is applied to an invariant bounded orbit.

title: Bi-Lipschitz equivalence and the cube--sphere example
notes: The discussion uses Lipschitz equivalence and compares piecewise-smooth and smooth shapes.

title: Characteristic information from measurable metric data

title: Full dual pairs versus commuting subalgebras
notes: Mutually commuting pullbacks are called a dual pair.
statement: For Poisson submersions from a symplectic manifold, a full dual pair requires \((\ker dJ_1)^\omega=\ker dJ_2\). Merely requiring all pullbacks from the two targets to commute gives only an inclusion; global mutual-centralizer conclusions require suitable connected-fibre hypotheses.
fate: This distinction belongs to the earlier dual-pair theory, checked through Weinstein's survey and the speaker's 1985 use of it. The notebook omits necessary rank and fullness qualifications.

title: Local symplectic-leaf correspondence in a dual pair
notes: A preimage under one arrow maps to a leaf under the other.
statement: For a full dual pair with the required submersion/rank assumptions, the image of a connected local preimage of a leaf under one map lies in and locally fills a leaf of the other. Identifying complete global leaves requires further completeness and fibre hypotheses.

title: The Lie-bialgebra double and its group
notes: The vector sum of a Lie algebra and its dual is given a compatible bracket.
statement: The double \(\mathfrak d=\mathfrak g\oplus\mathfrak g^*\) has the canonical split pairing and the bracket determined by invariance together with the brackets on its two isotropic summands. Passing to groups requires choosing integrations and a factorization domain.
fate: Drinfeld (1983), Theorem 2 and its integration discussion, predates the talk. A Lie-algebra direct sum as vector spaces need not be a direct product of Lie algebras.

title: Coisotropic invariant functions: sufficiency but not a single-action converse
notes: The invariant-subalgebra criterion is stated with an if-and-only-if.
statement: If \(H\) is connected and \(\mathfrak h^\perp\) is a Lie subalgebra of \(\mathfrak g^*\), then \(C^\infty(M)^H\) is Poisson-closed for every Poisson--Lie action. Necessity fails for a fixed action: a trivial action has every function invariant, regardless of \(H\).
fate: The sufficient direction is Semenov-Tian-Shansky (1985), Theorem 6. The chapter supplies a full noncoisotropic connected-subgroup counterexample using the additive group with \(\pi=z\partial_x\wedge\partial_y\), independently checked.

title: Quantization of Poisson--Lie/Lie-bialgebra structures
notes: The lecture ends with a quantum or deformation direction.
